# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Missingness shows up in many real-life scenarios, arising fro different sources like improper data collection, malfunctioning equipment, or operational data loss. In all these scenarios, imputation is a well-accepted standard technique to regularise available data in order to perform conventional machine learning or deep-learning analyses. However, it is well-known that all types of imputation induce biases in the data that can negatively impact the downstream task, and improvements in the quality of imputation do not necessarily result in improvement in downstream task performance. In this thesis, I will argue that approaches to performing downstream tasks without imputation can outperform imputation methods. In cases where this is not possible, I will argue that adapting simple imputation methods to also keep the downstream task in mind can result in better imputation than a separated impute-then-classify type procedure. Finally, I will extend these arguments to more complex structures than simple tabular data or time-series data, with an example of networks with missing node labels.
